meta.onePayoff: Every pip command translated, pip-tools replaced by compile and sync, and the handful of places uv is deliberately stricter.

seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #12 — Every pip Command, Translated (2026)
altTitles: Migrating from pip and pip-tools to uv
seo.description: Chapter twelve of the uv course. The uv pip interface, uv venv, compile and sync replacing pip-tools, the -o trap that catches everyone, migrating requirements.txt into pyproject.toml, and where uv is deliberately stricter than pip.

scenes.narration: You already know pip. Nearly every command you know still works.

Put the word uv in front of any pip command you've ever typed, and the command works. Same flags, same arguments, same shape of output. So why bother at all? Because the install that took pip eleven seconds takes under a second and a half here — and because uv catches things pip waves straight through.

uvStage.headline: Put [uv] in front of it
uvStage.premise: The pip interface is deliberately familiar. Same flags, same shapes, faster.

steps.label: pip install rich
steps.detail: the command you already know

steps.label: uv pip install rich
steps.detail: same command, one word in front

steps.label: uv pip list | wc -l
steps.detail: and the same four packages, either way

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter is a translation guide for everything you already know, plus the handful of places where uv is deliberately stricter than pip and will tell you so.

data.title: Coming from pip
data.subtitle: uv, chapter twelve · the translation, and the sharp edges

scenes.narration: Start with the door that looks exactly like the one you came through.

Install, list, freeze, show, uninstall — every one of them exists, and every one behaves the way you'd expect. There's a tree command too, which pip has no equivalent for and which you'll reach for far more often than you'd guess.

uvStage.headline: The commands you [already] type
uvStage.premise: Five familiar commands, plus one pip never had.

steps.label: uv pip list
steps.detail: exactly the shape pip prints

steps.label: uv pip tree
steps.detail: and this one pip simply does not have

scenes.narration: Then there's uv venv, which replaces python dash m venv and does two things that command never did. First it names the interpreter it borrowed, so you know what you got. Second it prints the activation line for the shell you're actually in, which saves a search every single time you forget the Windows spelling.

uvStage.headline: uv venv, [and] the extras
uvStage.premise: The same folder as python -m venv, plus two things that command never says.

steps.label: uv venv
steps.detail: it names the interpreter, and the command

steps.label: python -m venv .venv2
steps.detail: the old way. silent, and no gitignore.

stage.label: pyvenv.cfg
stage.sub: the six lines from chapter eight

scenes.narration: Now the pair that replaces a whole separate tool.

If you've used pip-tools, this pair will look immediately familiar. Compile turns a loose list of requirements into an exact pinned one. Sync then makes your environment match that pinned list precisely. Both live inside uv already, which means there's nothing extra to install and nothing else to keep updated.

uvStage.headline: pip-tools, [built in]
uvStage.premise: compile turns a loose list into a pinned one. sync makes the folder match it.

steps.label: cat requirements.in
steps.detail: one loose line, no version at all

steps.label: uv pip compile requirements.in -o requirements.txt
steps.detail: and four exact ones come out

stage.label: pygments
stage.sub: and every line records who asked

scenes.narration: And here's a trap that catches almost everybody the first time. Compile prints its output. Compile does not write a file unless you pass dash o. So a beginner runs the documented command, sees the result scroll past, goes looking for requirements dot txt, and finds nothing there.

uvStage.headline: It [prints]. It does not write.
uvStage.premise: Without -o the compiled output goes to your screen, and no file is created.

steps.label: uv pip compile requirements.in
out: # This file was autogenerated by uv via the following command:
steps.detail: printed. nothing was saved.

steps.label: ls requirements.txt
out: ls: cannot access requirements.txt: No such file
steps.detail: exactly as promised, and as surprising

scenes.narration: Those little via comments are worth reading, by the way. Every pinned line records who asked for it. Via rich means rich needed it. Via dash r requirements dot in means you did. Which turns a wall of pins into something you can actually audit.

uvStage.headline: Each line records [who asked]
uvStage.premise: via rich means rich needed it. via -r means you did. That distinction is auditable.

steps.label: cat requirements.txt
steps.detail: three pins, three different reasons

scenes.narration: One more distinction, and it mirrors chapter nine. uv pip install adds to whatever is already there. uv pip sync makes the environment match the file exactly, which means anything not in that file gets removed. Install is additive. Sync is exact. Reach for the right one.

uvStage.headline: Install adds. Sync is [exact].
uvStage.premise: One leaves what it finds. The other makes the folder match the file, and only it.

steps.label: uv pip install typer && uv pip sync requirements.txt
steps.detail: added, then removed by the very next command

stage.label: rich
stage.sub: and the folder now matches exactly

scenes.narration: Now the migration itself, which is genuinely two commands.

Run uv init on the folder you already have, then uv add dash r pointing at your requirements file. uv reads every line and writes each one into pyproject properly. Point dash c at your pinned file as well, and uv keeps the exact versions you were already running — because a migration that changes your versions isn't a migration, it's an upgrade in disguise.

uvStage.headline: Two commands, [one] migration
uvStage.premise: Adopt the folder, then read your requirements into pyproject with the pins kept.

steps.label: uv init --bare
steps.detail: adopt the folder you already have

steps.label: uv add -r requirements.in -c requirements.txt
steps.detail: and the pins you had are the pins you keep

stage.label: uv.lock
stage.sub: and the whole thing is one file now

scenes.narration: The mapping is easy to hold. Your loose requirements file becomes project dependencies. Your pinned file becomes the lockfile. And any dev requirements file becomes a dependency group, which is what chapter seven called the development group.

uvStage.headline: What becomes [what]
uvStage.premise: Three familiar files, three new homes, and nothing lost in the move.

steps.label: uv add -r requirements-dev.txt --dev
steps.detail: straight into the dev group

stage.label: pyproject.toml
stage.sub: what your project can live with

scenes.narration: And finally, the places where uv will not do what pip did.

The documentation puts it plainly: uv is stricter than pip, and will often reject packages that pip would happily install. None of that is uv being difficult. Broken metadata pip waved through becomes a problem you find weeks later, and later is always more expensive than now.

uvStage.headline: uv stops what [pip waves] through
uvStage.premise: The same package, offered to both. Only one of them reads the small print.

steps.label: uv pip install broken-metadata
out: x Failed to parse metadata for broken-metadata==1.0.0
Caused by: expected a version specifier
steps.detail: refused, and it says exactly why

stage.label: uv
stage.detail: stricter, and it tells you now

scenes.narration: Three differences will actually bite you. uv has no dash dash user install. uv ignores pip dot conf and the pip index environment variable, using its own settings instead. And uv wants a virtual environment rather than installing into the system Python.

uvStage.headline: Three that will [bite]
uvStage.premise: Not a list of all eighteen. These three are the ones a beginner actually hits.

steps.label: uv pip install --user rich
steps.detail: no --user. use a venv, or a tool.

stage.label: --user
stage.sub: a venv or uv tool install instead

stage.label: pip.conf
stage.sub: uv reads its own config files

stage.label: a venv
stage.sub: and uv will make one for you

scenes.narration: And here's one that surprises even experienced people. Upper bounds on requires-python are ignored entirely. If a package claims to need Python below three point twelve, uv treats the claim as advice rather than law — because such upper bounds are almost always wrong, and they age very badly indeed.

uvStage.headline: Upper bounds are [ignored]
uvStage.premise: requires-python upper bounds age badly, so uv treats them as advice.

steps.label: uv pip install "old-package"
steps.detail: installed, despite claiming <3.12

scenes.narration: One habit worth changing while you're here. In the pip world you'd activate an environment and then type pip install. With uv you can skip the activation entirely, because uv finds the environment for you — which is chapter eight's lesson arriving in a place you didn't expect it.

uvStage.headline: Stop [activating] first
uvStage.premise: The pip interface finds your environment the same way uv run does.

steps.label: uv pip install rich
steps.detail: it found the .venv without being told

stage.label: uv pip install rich
stage.sub: no activation, and the right shelf

scenes.narration: A word on when to use which interface, because having both can be confusing. The pip commands are a bridge: perfect for an existing project, a quick experiment, or a script somebody else wrote. For anything you'll maintain, use the project commands instead, because those give you the lockfile.

uvStage.headline: A bridge, not a [destination]
uvStage.premise: The pip interface is for what already exists. The project commands are for what you keep.

steps.label: uv pip install rich && ls uv.lock
out: ls: cannot access uv.lock: No such file
steps.detail: the pip interface writes no lockfile

stage.label: uv pip install
stage.sub: an existing project, or an experiment

stage.label: uv.lock
stage.sub: and only the project commands write it

scenes.narration: Finally, two things you'll want on day one of any migration. uv pip check reports anything inconsistent, exactly like the pip command from chapter zero. And uv pip freeze still prints what's installed, so you can compare against the file you started with.

uvStage.headline: Check, then [compare]
uvStage.premise: Two familiar commands, useful for proving a migration changed nothing.

steps.label: uv pip check
steps.detail: the readout nobody ran, in chapter zero

steps.label: uv pip freeze | diff requirements.txt -
steps.detail: no output means nothing changed at all

scenes.narration: Quick check. You run uv pip compile on a requirements file and then look for the output file. Is it there? Pause the video here and answer for yourself before I say it. Ready? No — compile prints to your screen unless you pass dash o.

quiz.question: uv pip compile ran. Is requirements.txt on disk?
quiz.why: Without -o the compiled output goes to stdout and no file is written.

scenes.narration: So, to recap. Every pip command you know works with uv in front of it. Compile and sync replace pip-tools outright, and compile prints unless you ask it to write. And uv is deliberately stricter, which costs you a refusal now instead of a mystery later.

points.text: Put uv in front. Everything still works.
compile prints — pass -o to write a file
Stricter now beats a mystery later

scenes.narration: Last chapter next: turning what you've built into something anybody in the world can install with one command.
